paras: The attempted lynching of Emma Johnson took place at Summerfield, Georgia, about six miles from Macon, in March 1882, when a mob surrounded the officers holding Johnson, a young Black woman accused of killing a local merchant. The officers prevented the lynching and took her to Macon, where she was later convicted of murder in Bibb Superior Court. Papers across the country carried the story as a murder, with the mob mentioned in a single sentence.

According to a Macon dispatch of March 15, William A. Evans, an elderly merchant of Summerfield, was killed in bed in his store on the night of March 14 by blows from an axe struck in the dark. Johnson, who also went by Carrie Massey, was accused of the killing; the wire report said Evans had "kindly given" her a night's lodging and that robbery was her object, but that his groans brought help. The Savannah Morning News described her as "about sixteen years old" and wrote that she "persistently denies any connection with the crime."

Johnson was arrested and held by officers at Summerfield. There, according to every version of the dispatch, the officers "were surrounded by a mob of white and colored people, but by strenuous efforts lynching was prevented." No injury to her and no attempt to seize her is described, and the size of the mob is not given. She was then brought to Macon, on the morning, afternoon or evening of March 15 depending on the copy, and was held in jail.

No arrests of anyone in the mob were reported. The case of the State against Carrie Massey was marked for trial at Macon in late May, and the Macon Telegraph and Messenger, as quoted by the Savannah paper, predicted it would be one of the most interesting of the term because "there is much more in it than has been given to the public." A dispatch dated Summerfield, May 31, said she had been convicted the day before and sentenced to be hanged on a day the governor would set. The Savannah Morning News reported on June 12 that Judge Simmons had instead sentenced her to life in the penitentiary, saying that because the evidence was "entirely circumstantial" the law let him commute the sentence even though the jury had not recommended mercy.

Coverage came entirely from the white press, and all of the March reports trace to Macon dispatches that print the same sentence about the mob. The Savannah Morning News ran the story under "An Old Man Butchered by a Young Negress" among other Macon news, calling her "the murderess" and the evidence "conclusive." The wire version ran in the Dallas Daily Herald, the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer and the Richmond Dispatch on March 16, in the Knoxville Daily Chronicle on March 17 and in the Somerset Herald on March 29. Headlines focused on the killing and on Evans's hospitality, as in the Richmond paper's "A Diabolical Georgia Murder," whose subhead alone, "Lynch Law Threatened," pointed to the mob.

The copies differ on details: the Dallas and Knoxville papers named the merchant W. R. Evans, the Dallas paper printed her alias as "Carrie Wassey" and the Richmond paper as "Carrie Massie," and the Lancaster paper placed Macon in Pennsylvania. A Pennsylvania weekly later announced her conviction under the headline "A Young Girl to be Hanged," calling her "a very pretty girl" of seventeen.

Reports of her sentence conflict: the May 31 dispatch gave death by hanging, while the later Savannah report gave life imprisonment and the judge's reasons for it, which makes it the better evidence on the final sentence.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Emma Johnson
bases: A mob surrounded the officers holding a Black woman accused of murder at Summerfield and a lynching was 'prevented' (A1, A2, A4); no one was killed, so this is an averted lynching.

A mob threatened to lynch Emma Johnson over an accused murder, but officers prevented it and she was taken to Macon alive (A1, A2, A4); she was later tried and sentenced in court (A8, A9), so no one was killed and the episode is an attempted lynching.

The mob scene is known only from March 15 Macon dispatches that print the same sentence about it word for word (A1, A2, A3, A4), so they appear to share one source; the murder accusation itself is confirmed by the later trial reports (A7, A8, A9).

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News Macon correspondent
accounts.gist: Evans was killed with an axe in his store 'for the sake of plunder'; Johnson denied it but 'the evidence is conclusive'; officers were surrounded by a mob and a lynching was prevented.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Evans had 'kindly' given the woman a night's lodging; robbery was her object but his groans brought help; she was arrested and taken to Macon after officers held off a mob of white and colored people.

accounts.label: Trial reports
accounts.gist: Carrie Massey was tried in Bibb Superior Court and convicted; the sentence was reported as death (A8) and as life imprisonment on circumstantial evidence (A9).

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News ran it as one item in 'Flashes from Macon' under 'An Old Man Butchered by a Young Negress', calling her 'the murderess' and the evidence 'conclusive'.
Wire copies stressed her ingratitude ('to whom Evans had kindly given a night's lodging'); the Richmond Dispatch headlined 'A Diabolical Georgia Murder ... Lynch Law Threatened'.
Papers in Texas, Pennsylvania and Tennessee carried the same dispatch with small variations in names.
